clue.text: Dryden's Alexander's Feast suitable for Bond play?

definitions.text: Dryden's Alexander's Feast suitable for Bond play?

parts.words: Dryden's Alexander's Feast suitable for Bond play?
parts.note: the Alexander is taken to be the poet Alexander Pope, and a feast for him would be a marriage celebration, which is the title of an Edward Bond play

explanation.surface: A query about whether Dryden's ode could be staged as a play by Edward Bond.
explanation.walkthrough: Dryden's ode is about Alexander the Great; the clue swaps in the other famous Alexander, the poet Pope, and turns his feast into a wedding banquet. Edward Bond's first play has that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Bond's 1962 play takes its title from a papal marriage feast, the occasion the clue describes.

clue.text: Rescue old garment for The Vicar of Bray?

explanation.surface: Mending an old jacket for a famous clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: To turn a coat is to unpick it and resew it inside out so a worn garment can be worn again. The Vicar of Bray, in the old song, changed his religion with every new monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Reversing a worn jacket's cloth salvages it, and the song's vicar is the classic deserter who switched sides to keep his living.

clue.text: Something nasty concealed by the paper in Christie novel?

parts.note: wickedness, something nasty, is evil
a thing concealed by another lies under it
The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: Something unpleasant is buried inside a newspaper, as in a detective story.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper. Agatha Christie's Poirot mystery is set at a Devon holiday hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: A 1941 Hercule Poirot mystery by Agatha Christie carries this title.

clue.text: Segal sequel hero or waif

explanation.surface: A hero from Erich Segal's follow-up book, or a homeless child.
explanation.definitionFit: Erich Segal's sequel to Love Story is Oliver's Story, about Oliver Barrett; Dickens's workhouse orphan Twist is literature's best-known waif.

clue.text: The Amis one was fat

parts.note: Kingsley Amis wrote a 1963 novel titled 'One Fat' followed by a word for a man from England

explanation.surface: A remark that one of the Amis family was overweight.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley Amis's novel One Fat Englishman follows an overweight Briton in America; the clue rearranges the title's words.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Kingsley Amis's novel describes a corpulent man from England, the noun the clue leaves out.

clue.text: Direction from which to expect the return of the soldier

definitions.text: from which to expect the return of the soldier

explanation.surface: Which compass point a returning soldier should be expected from.
explanation.walkthrough: Rebecca West wrote the 1918 novel The Return of the Soldier, so that book comes 'from' her.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a compass point, and also the surname of Rebecca, the author of the novel The Return of the Soldier.

clue.text: Let in sort of light for Woolf character

indicators.note: 'in' asks for the word for let to be set inside the word for the light

parts.note: daylight is one sort of light, so day stands for it
to let something happen is to allow it

explanation.surface: Opening a window for daylight on behalf of a Virginia Woolf heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; 'sort of light' wants to describe a lamp but stands for daylight. Clarissa is the title character of Virginia Woolf's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarissa, the society hostess of Virginia Woolf's 1925 novel, carries this surname.

clue.text: Exciting Stuart book possibly as Bizet creation

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the letters of the following words could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A thriller that might have been composed by the man who wrote Carmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges ASBIZETCREATION. Alistair Stuart MacLean wrote the Arctic submarine thriller; 'Bizet creation' wants to suggest an opera, but it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Alistair Stuart MacLean's 1963 Cold War thriller, about a submarine racing to an Arctic base, is this title.

clue.text: Playwright in Britain known as Lawrence

parts.note: GB is the abbreviation for Great Britain
T. E. Lawrence enlisted under the assumed name Shaw

explanation.surface: A dramatist in Britain who went by the name Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawrence of Arabia changed his name to Shaw in the 1920s, so a playwright with initials G B and that surname fits.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard wrote Pygmalion and Saint Joan, and is often called by his initials and surname.

clue.text: Uplifting experience for Salinger artisans

parts.note: Salinger's title Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters gives the artisans their uplifting task

explanation.surface: Something that cheers up craftsmen in a Salinger story.
explanation.walkthrough: J. D. Salinger's novella Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters orders its craftsmen to lift a beam, so for them the experience is literally uplifting.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting a roof beam is a hoisting job, which is what Salinger's title asks of the carpenters.

clue.text: Marketeers from Twain's Golden Age?

explanation.surface: Traders who appear in a Mark Twain novel about a golden era.
explanation.walkthrough: Twain's novel is really The Gilded Age; 'Golden' loosely stands for it, and its schemer is Colonel Beriah Sellers.
explanation.definitionFit: Marketeers are vendors; Colonel Beriah of that surname is the speculator in Twain and Warner's The Gilded Age, so the plural names him and his kin.

clue.text: Pure coin debased for composer

indicators.note: debased money has been altered, so the letters of the coin words are altered in order

explanation.surface: Unalloyed money gets adulterated, to a composer's cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'debased' rearranges PURECOIN.
explanation.definitionFit: François, the French Baroque harpsichordist, is a famous composer with this surname.

clue.text: She was richly left

parts.note: echoes Bassanio's line in The Merchant of Venice, 'In Belmont is a lady richly left'

explanation.surface: A woman who inherited a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice, Bassanio describes the heiress of Belmont as 'a lady richly left', meaning her father left her a fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: The wealthy heiress of Belmont in The Merchant of Venice is the lady Bassanio describes.

clue.text: "When we died they said, 'Our — were low'." (Randall Jarrell)

definitions.text: "When we died they said, 'Our — were low'." (Randall Jarrell)

parts.words: "When we died they said, 'Our — were low'." (Randall Jarrell)
parts.note: the missing word completes a line from Jarrell's war poem 'Losses', about airmen killed in training

explanation.surface: A line of war poetry with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Randall Jarrell's poem 'Losses', about American airmen killed in the Second World War; the gap is the military word for the dead and wounded.
explanation.definitionFit: Military reports count the dead and wounded as losses, the word the poem's officials used to make the deaths sound small.

clue.text: Much-capped character from Scotland Yard

indicators.note: 'from' says the name is taken out of the run of letters across the next two words

explanation.surface: A frequently capped footballer from the Metropolitan Police headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes the answer out of scotlAND Yard. Andy Capp is a long-running British newspaper cartoon character, a flat-capped northern working man; 'much-capped' wants to mean a sports international.
explanation.definitionFit: Andy Capp, the cartoon layabout who always wears a flat cap, bears this first name.

clue.text: Sydney Smith suggested two of them as "the thirty-nine times articled clerk"

definitions.text: Sydney Smith suggested two of them as "the thirty-nine times articled clerk"

parts.words: Sydney Smith suggested two of them as "the thirty-nine times articled clerk"
parts.note: the clergyman-wit Sydney Smith joked about a gift of game birds to a cleric bound by the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England

explanation.surface: A Regency wit proposing a gift for an Anglican clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: Anglican clergy had to assent to the Thirty-Nine Articles, so a clerk 'articled' thirty-nine times is a clergyman; Sydney Smith tied his wit about such a cleric to a brace of game birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Game birds shot for the table, traditionally given in a brace, are what a country parson might expect as a gift.

clue.text: Incomparable black medick press

explanation.surface: An unrivalled clover-like plant and a printing house.
explanation.walkthrough: Black medick is a small yellow-flowered clover relative, and the Nonesuch Press was a fine-edition English publisher founded in 1923.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old word for something unrivalled, a country name for the plant Medicago lupulina, and the name of a London private publishing house.

clue.text: In such a chapel, history was now and England for Eliot

definitions.text: In such a chapel, history was now and England for Eliot

parts.words: In such a chapel, history was now and England for Eliot
parts.note: recalls the close of Eliot's Little Gidding: 'in a ___ chapel / History is now and England'

explanation.surface: A remark on a chapel where past and present met for T. S. Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: The last section of T. S. Eliot's Little Gidding sets its moment of revelation in a remote chapel on a winter afternoon, where 'History is now and England'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's quiet, remote chapel at Little Gidding is described with this word for hidden away.

clue.text: Eminence inspiring Milton's attack on censor ship

definitions.text: inspiring Milton's attack on censor ship

explanation.surface: A hill that prompted Milton's polemic against official censorship.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's 1644 pamphlet against licensing books, Areopagitica, takes its name from the Athenian hill where the council met.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the rocky hill in Athens, an eminence, and the source of the title of Milton's attack on censorship.

clue.text: Wishful thinking, perhaps, for Brookner's Edith

explanation.surface: Daydreaming that might suit a character in Anita Brookner's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Edith is the romantic novelist at the centre of Anita Brookner's Booker-winning Hotel du Lac.
explanation.definitionFit: Wishful thinking is optimistic expectation; Brookner's heroine in Hotel du Lac is Edith of that surname.

clue.text: Shakespearean knight uses small capitals, gets poor return

parts.note: s.c. is the printer's abbreviation for small capitals

indicators.note: 'return' says the word poor is to be read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A knight in Shakespeare writes in little capital letters and gets a bad response.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns POOR into ROOP. Sir Stephen Scroop appears in Richard II, Lord Scroop in Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Stephen of this name brings Richard II bad news in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Sagan would have had our opinion of him

definitions.text: Sagan would have had our opinion of him

parts.words: Sagan would have had our opinion of him
parts.note: Françoise Sagan's novel title asks the reader 'Do you like ...?' about a composer

explanation.surface: A suggestion that Françoise Sagan wanted to know what we thought of a man.
explanation.walkthrough: Françoise Sagan's novel Aimez-vous Brahms? (Do you like Brahms?) asks for the reader's opinion of a composer in its very title.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagan's title names the German Romantic composer whose music the reader is asked about.

clue.text: One of Valéry's about yesterday in France?

parts.note: ca. (circa) is the abbreviation for about
hier is French for yesterday

explanation.surface: One of Paul Valéry's things concerning the day before, in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Valéry kept notebooks every morning for fifty years, published as his Cahiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Valéry's private notebooks are called his Cahiers, French for exercise books, so one is a single volume of them.

clue.text: His love was lost in A Winter's Tale

definitions.text: His love was lost in A Winter's Tale

parts.words: His love was lost in A Winter's Tale
parts.note: the prince's beloved in The Winter's Tale is Perdita, whose name means the lost one

explanation.surface: A man whose sweetheart went missing in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Perdita, abandoned as a baby, takes her name from the Latin for 'lost'; the Bohemian prince loves her.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bohemian prince who woos Perdita in The Winter's Tale bears this name.

clue.text: Prospero's was weather-fended by a time-grove

definitions.text: Prospero's was weather-fended by a time-grove

parts.words: Prospero's was weather-fended by a time-grove
parts.note: quotes The Tempest, where Ariel says the prisoners are 'in the line-grove which weather-fends your' dwelling

explanation.surface: Prospero's room was shielded from the weather by trees.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Tempest V.i Ariel tells Prospero the prisoners wait 'in the line-grove which weather-fends your cell'; the page prints 'time-grove' for Shakespeare's 'line-grove', a grove of lime trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero lives in a small room cut in the rock, which the play calls by the word for a monk's or prisoner's chamber.

clue.text: "1 strive to be brief, and become " (Horace)

definitions.text: "1 strive to be brief, and become " (Horace)

parts.words: "1 strive to be brief, and become " (Horace)
parts.note: Horace's Ars Poetica: 'brevis esse laboro, obscurus fio', the cost of over-compression

explanation.surface: A line from Horace with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Horace warns in the Ars Poetica that a writer who strives for brevity becomes unclear: 'brevis esse laboro, obscurus fio'. The '1' is the printed 'I'.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace's Latin 'obscurus' means hard to understand, and the English word for unclear completes the line.

clue.text: Irving character in which a boding was felt

indicators.note: 'in' says the name sits inside the next words of the clue

explanation.surface: A character of Washington Irving's who sensed a foreboding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the name inside wICH A BODing. Ichabod Crane is the schoolmaster of Irving's The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, fittingly full of foreboding.
explanation.definitionFit: Ichabod Crane, the nervous schoolmaster of The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, carries this first name.

clue.text: Chaplain's lads in disarray in Unsworth book The Crossword is available on the Internet, at www the website will be eligible for the prize.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held runs into competition text ('The Crossword is available on the Internet...'); the anagram fodder 'Chaplain's lads' cannot give the grid's PANCHALISISLAND, and Unsworth's book is Pascali's Island, so clue and answer are both garbled.
